title: The simile of light reflected from water
greek: sicut aquae tremulum labris ubi lumen aenis / sole repercussum aut radiantis imagine lunae / omnia pervolitat late loca
short: Aeneas' anxious, darting thoughts are compared to sunlight or moonlight reflected from water in a bronze basin, flickering over a room up to the ceiling.
body: Conington traces the simile to Apollonius Rhodius 3.755-760, where Medea's heart flutters like a sunbeam reflected from water poured into a cauldron, and notes possible echoes of Lucretius. He thinks the image suits Medea's lovesick heart better than a general's planning. Others find it exact: the light is bright, restless and unable to settle, just like Aeneas' mind, which 'throws this way and that' (huc ... illuc). The image also prepares for the calm that follows when the Tiber god appears. A woman's love in Apollonius becomes a leader's worry in Virgil, a typical transformation of a Hellenistic model.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 8.22 (Apollonius 3.756 ff.)

anchor: the very god of the ground
title: Tiberinus, the river-god of the Tiber
greek: huic deus ipse loci fluvio Tiberinus amoeno / populeas inter senior se attollere frondes / visus
short: The god of the Tiber rises from his river in a dream, old, veiled in grey linen and crowned with reeds, to reassure Aeneas and send him to Evander.
body: River-gods were pictured as old men, and Conington notes the conventions: the grey linen robe (carbasus) stands for his waters and the reed crown for his banks. He calls himself 'glassy Tiber, best beloved by heaven of rivers' and 'the horned river', since river-gods were often shown with horns (the roar and force of a bull). The scene mirrors earlier dream-visions (Hector in 2.268-297, Mercury in 4.554-570) but is wholly reassuring: 'here is thine assured home'. Aeneas' prayer at dawn, scooping water in his hands (8.68-78), is a correct Roman ritual address to a local deity. Ennius had already invoked 'father Tiberinus', a phrase Virgil echoes at 9.816.

title: The white sow and her thirty piglets
greek: litoreis ingens inventa sub ilicibus sus / triginta capitum fetus enixa iacebit, / alba
short: The promised white sow with thirty white piglets confirms the dream: Ascanius will found Alba ('the white town') after thirty years.
body: The sign was first foretold by Helenus at 3.389-393. Conington, following Varro, explains the symbolism: the white (alba) sow stands for Alba Longa, and the thirty piglets for the thirty years between the founding of Lavinium and of Alba (Jupiter's prophecy had already given Ascanius thirty years at 1.267-271). He notes a slight confusion, since in Book III the omen marks the site of Lavinium. The sow and piglets were a famous Lavinian image; a bronze sow was shown at Lavinium in Varro's day. Aeneas offers the sow to Juno (8.84-85), a pointed act of piety toward his enemy, in line with the Tiber's command to appease her.

title: Pallanteum, Evander's Arcadian town
greek: Arcades his oris, genus a Pallante profectum, / qui regem Evandrum comites, qui signa secuti, / delegere locum et posuere in montibus urbem / Pallantis proavi de nomine Pallanteum
short: Evander's Arcadian colony on the Palatine hill is named after his ancestor Pallas; the name was believed to be the origin of 'Palatium', the Palatine.
body: Roman antiquarians derived the Palatine (Palatium) from Pallantion, a town in Arcadia from which Evander came (Livy 1.5.1; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Roman Antiquities 1.31). Virgil makes Aeneas sail up the Tiber to the future site of Rome itself, so that Book VIII becomes a tour of Rome before Rome: a poor town where the Palatine (in Virgil's day the site of Augustus' house and the temple of Apollo) stands. Conington notes that one tradition makes Pallas son of Lycaon and founder of Pallantion. Evander's son, also called Pallas, will be entrusted to Aeneas, and his death at Turnus' hands (10.479-505) leads to the poem's last scene.

title: The Ara Maxima and the cult of Hercules
greek: hanc aram luco statuit, quae maxima semper / dicetur nobis et erit quae maxima semper
short: Evander's people are honouring Hercules at the 'Greatest Altar' (Ara Maxima), the ancient Roman altar of Hercules in the cattle market, when the Trojans arrive.
body: The Ara Maxima stood in the Forum Boarium, Rome's cattle market by the Tiber, and was one of the city's oldest cults. Livy tells the same story of Hercules and Cacus and says this was the only foreign rite Romulus adopted, and that the families of the Potitii and Pinarii served it (1.7.3-15); Livy later records that the Potitii died out after the cult was handed to public slaves in 312 BC (9.29.9-11). Conington notes that the altar's position by the cattle market 'must have helped to suggest the story' of the stolen cattle. Worshippers crowned themselves with poplar, Hercules' tree (Eclogue 7.61). The 'son of Amphitryon' is Hercules, legally son of Amphitryon but really of Jupiter; 'Alcides' (grandson of Alcaeus) is the same hero.

title: Aeneas' appeal to kinship through Atlas
greek: Dardanus, Iliacae primus pater urbis et auctor, / Electra, ut Grai perhibent, Atlantide cretus ... / vobis Mercurius pater est ...
short: Aeneas wins Evander's alliance by tracing both their families to Atlas: Dardanus was son of Atlas' daughter Electra, Mercury son of Atlas' daughter Maia.
body: Aeneas approaches a Greek, kin of 'the twin sons of Atreus', so he argues from genealogy, a classic diplomatic move in Greek and Roman politics (states often claimed shared ancestors to justify alliances). Electra and Maia were both Pleiades, daughters of Atlas. Dardanus was son of Zeus and Electra; Evander, in Virgil's version, is son of Mercury (Hermes), whom Maia bore on Mount Cyllene in Arcadia. Conington notes that sources differ on Evander's parentage (Livy and others make the prophetess Carmentis his mother, as Virgil also does at 8.336). Aeneas comes in person as a suppliant with olive branches 'dressed in fillets' (vitta comptos ... ramos, 8.128), the formal sign of supplication. Evander answers with a personal memory of the young Anchises (8.154-171), so the alliance rests on old guest-friendship as well as blood.

title: Superstitio
greek: non haec sollemnia nobis, / has ex more dapes, hanc tanti numinis aram / vana superstitio veterumque ignara deorum / imposuit
short: Evander insists that his rites for Hercules are not 'empty superstition' ignorant of the old gods, but gratitude for a real deliverance.
body: Latin superstitio meant excessive or misdirected religious fear, as opposed to religio, proper observance. Conington explains vana superstitio as an empty feeling, with no root in old belief, that 'catches blindly' at new cults, and suggests that Virgil reflects his own age's suspicion of foreign, especially Eastern, gods (compare the monstrous Egyptian gods on the shield, 8.698). Evander's rite is justified because it commemorates an event: Hercules saved the community from Cacus. This mirrors the Augustan programme of restoring ancient Roman cults. Cicero discusses the distinction between superstitio and religio in De Natura Deorum 2.71-72.

title: Hercules and Cacus
greek: hic spelunca fuit vasto summota recessu, / semihominis Caci facies quam dira tenebat
short: Evander tells how Hercules killed Cacus, a fire-breathing, half-human son of Vulcan who stole the hero's cattle and hid them in his cave on the Aventine.
body: The story appears also in Livy (1.7), Propertius (4.9) and Ovid (Fasti 1.543-586), and Conington notes that Ovid clearly copied Virgil. Cacus drags the cattle backwards by their tails so their tracks mislead; a lowing heifer betrays him. Virgil makes the fight cosmic: Hercules tears away a crag so that light floods into the den 'as though some force ... should unlock the infernal house' (8.243-246). Many scholars read the episode as a mythic type of Rome's history: the saviour hero defeating a monster of violence and darkness anticipates Aeneas defeating Turnus and Augustus defeating Antony. Octavian's triple triumph of 29 BC (shown at 8.714) has often been linked with this story of a hero's victory and sacrifice. G. K. Galinsky's study traces these links. Readers have also noticed that Hercules' furor and ira resemble Aeneas' rage at the end of the poem.

title: The Salii sing Hercules' praises
greek: tum Salii ad cantus incensa altaria circum / populeis adsunt evincti tempora ramis
short: The Salii, two choirs of young and old, sing a hymn to Hercules listing his labours: an archaic Roman priesthood transferred to Evander's rite.
body: At Rome the Salii were the 'leaping' priests of Mars who danced through the city in March carrying the sacred ancilia (shields) and chanting an archaic hymn. Linking them to Hercules was unusual; Conington cites Macrobius (Saturnalia 3.12), who reports that pontiffs and Varro identified Hercules with Mars and that the Salii of Tibur served Hercules. The hymn is a compact catalogue of labours: the snakes strangled in the cradle, the sack of Troy and Oechalia, the Centaurs Hylaeus and Pholus, the Cretan bull, the Nemean lion, Cerberus, Typhoeus and the Lernaean Hydra, ending 'Hail, true seed of Jove'. Its form, with repeated 'thou' and 'thee', imitates Greek hymns. The dancing Salii also appear on Aeneas' shield (8.663).

anchor: chose Latium to be their name
title: Saturn in Latium and the golden age
greek: Latiumque vocari / maluit, his quoniam latuisset tutus in oris. / aurea quae perhibent illo sub rege fuere / saecula
short: Evander's history of Italy: wild tree-born men, then Saturn, exiled by Jupiter, hid (latuit) here and named the land Latium, ruling a golden age that decayed into war and greed.
body: Conington shows how Virgil blends Hesiod's ages of men with the succession of early Italian peoples. First come native Fauns and Nymphs and men 'born of stocks and hard oak' (an old idea of men sprung from trees or rocks). Saturn, fleeing Jupiter, gives them laws and calls the land Latium from latere, 'to hide', an etymology also found in Varro. His reign is the golden age, which slowly gives way to 'a sunken and stained time', the rage of war and 'the lust of possession' (amor habendi). Then the Ausonians and Sicani came, and the giant Thybris, from whom the river Albula took its name Tiber. The account is less idealised than Latinus' boast (7.202-204): the golden age lies in the past, and Anchises had prophesied that Augustus would restore it in Latium (6.792-794).

title: Carmentis and the Carmental Gate
greek: aram et Carmentalem Romani nomine portam / quam memorant, nymphae priscum Carmentis honorem, / vatis fatidicae
short: Evander's mother Carmentis was a prophetess; the Carmental Gate at the foot of the Capitol and her altar there preserved her memory.
body: Carmentis (or Carmenta) was an old Roman goddess of prophecy and childbirth, honoured at the Carmentalia in January. Her name was linked with carmen, 'song' or 'oracle', since prophecies were sung in verse. Livy (1.7.8) calls her a prophetess revered before the Sibyl came to Italy. Conington notes that the Carmental gate in the Servian wall was also known as the 'accursed gate', the one through which the Fabii marched out to their destruction at the Cremera. Virgil gives her the first prophecy of Rome's greatness on Roman soil: she 'sang of old the coming greatness of the Aeneadae'. This begins Evander's walking tour of the future city, in which almost every spot named is a famous Roman landmark.

title: The Asylum and the Lupercal
greek: hinc lucum ingentem, quem Romulus acer asylum / rettulit, et gelida monstrat sub rupe Lupercal / Parrhasio dictum Panos de more Lycaei
short: Evander shows Aeneas the grove that Romulus would make an asylum, and the Lupercal, the cave under the Palatine sacred to Lycaean Pan.
body: Romulus was said to have opened an asylum (sanctuary) on the Capitoline to attract settlers to his new city (Livy 1.8.5-6). The Lupercal was a cave at the foot of the Palatine where the she-wolf nursed Romulus and Remus (see the shield, 8.630-634). Conington notes the double etymology: Lupercal is linked to lupus, 'wolf', as Lycaeus is to Greek lykos, 'wolf'. 'Parrhasian' means Arcadian, and Pan Lycaeus was worshipped on Mount Lycaeus in Arcadia. Every February 15 the Lupercalia was celebrated from here, with young men (the Luperci) running round the Palatine. Augustus restored the Lupercal, which is one reason Virgil lingers on it.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 8.343 (Lupercal, lupus and Lycaeus; Parrhasius)
Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 1.8 (Romulus' asylum)

title: The Tarpeian rock and the golden Capitol
greek: hinc ad Tarpeiam sedem et Capitolia ducit / aurea nunc, olim silvestribus horrida dumis
short: Evander leads Aeneas to the Capitol, 'golden now, of old rough with forest thickets', where Jupiter was already felt to dwell.
body: The line contrasts then and now in a single phrase: the Capitol of Virgil's day, with the gilded roof of the temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus, was once a wooded hill. Conington notes that 'Tarpeius mons' was the old name of the Capitoline and cites Pliny (Natural History 33.57) on the gilding of the temple's bronze roof tiles under Q. Lutatius Catulus. The Arcadians already sense a god in the grove and believe they have seen Jupiter shaking his dark aegis to gather storms. This nostalgic 'then and now' technique runs through the whole tour, including the cattle lowing in the Forum and the fashionable district of the Carinae (8.360-361). Many readers sense both pride in Rome's greatness and regret for lost simplicity.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 8.347 (Tarpeius mons; Capitolia aurea, Pliny on the gilding)

title: 'Aude, hospes, contemnere opes'
greek: aude, hospes, contemnere opes et te quoque dignum / finge deo, rebusque veni non asper egenis
short: At his humble door Evander tells Aeneas to dare to despise wealth, and so to make himself worthy of a god, as Hercules did when he stayed here.
body: This is one of the moral centres of Book VIII. Hercules, who became a god by his labours, did not scorn this poor house; Aeneas must 'mould himself' (finge) to be worthy of godhead in the same way. Conington notes that aude expresses a moral effort, comparing Horace's sapere aude (Epistles 1.2.40). Seneca quotes the line in his letters (Epistles 18.12) as an exhortation to frugality. The scene of guest-friendship (hospitium) follows strict custom: a couch of leaves and a she-bear's skin for the guest in the narrow house. Virgil's Roman readers, living amid Augustan marble, are reminded that Rome's greatness began in poverty, a favourite theme of Roman moralists. Compare the thatched 'palace of Romulus' on the shield (8.654).

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 8.364 (aude; Horace's sapere aude)

title: Venus asks Vulcan for arms: Thetis and Aurora
greek: te filia Nerei, / te potuit lacrimis Tithonia flectere coniunx
short: Venus seduces her husband Vulcan into making armour for Aeneas, reminding him that he made arms for Thetis' son Akhilleus and for Aurora's son Memnon.
body: The scene combines two Homeric models, as Conington shows: Thetis' visit to Hephaestus to ask for arms for Akhilleus (Iliad 18.369 ff.) and Hera's seduction of Zeus (Iliad 14.159 ff.); Venus' language also recalls Lucretius' hymn to Venus (1.31-40). 'Nereus' daughter' is Thetis; 'Tithonus' consort' is Aurora (Eos), who obtained arms for Memnon in the lost epic Aethiopis. Conington notes the awkwardness of Venus begging her husband for armour for her son by another man, Anchises. Vulcan's surrender is compared to lightning splitting a cloud (8.391-392). The sequence makes Aeneas' new arms an answer to Akhilleus': the Trojan now gets divine armour as his great enemy once did.

title: The simile of the woman at her spinning
greek: cum femina primum, / cui tolerare colo vitam tenuique Minerva / impositum, cinerem et sopitos suscitat ignis
short: Vulcan rising before dawn is compared to a poor housewife who rekindles her fire at night and sets her maids spinning to keep her home chaste and fed.
body: The simile follows Vulcan's night of love with a picture of humble, virtuous labour, a deliberate contrast. Its ancestor is Iliad 12.433-435, where the balanced battle line is compared to a careful working woman weighing wool to earn a meagre wage for her children. Virgil turns the image into an emblem of the Roman matrona's ideals: chastity (castum ut servare cubile), industry and care for children. 'Slender Minerva' (tenuis Minerva) means the fine work of spinning, Minerva being goddess of crafts. The comparison suggests that the divine smith's work, like the woman's, sustains life and home; the armour he makes will protect Rome's future.

title: Vulcania and the Cyclopes' forge
greek: insula Sicanium iuxta latus Aeoliamque / erigitur Liparen ... / Volcani domus et Volcania nomine tellus. ... / Brontesque Steropesque et nudus membra Pyracmon
short: Vulcan's forge lies under Vulcania (Hiera, modern Vulcano) in the Aeolian islands, where the Cyclopes are hammering a thunderbolt, Mars' chariot and Minerva's aegis.
body: The volcanic island of Hiera near Lipari was believed to house Hephaestus' smithy; Thucydides reports that the locals thought so because of the fire and noise it gave off by night (3.88). The Cyclopes here are not Homer's cannibal shepherds but the smith-giants of Hesiod, who names three: Brontes ('Thunder'), Steropes ('Lightning') and Arges ('Bright'); Virgil replaces Arges with Pyracmon ('Fire-anvil'). The half-finished thunderbolt, made of 'three coils of frozen rain, three of watery mist, three of ruddy fire and winged south wind', is a playful technical description of a storm. The forge scene then builds to the making of Aeneas' shield, welded 'sevenfold, circle on circle', recalling the seven-layered shield of Ajax (Iliad 7.220).

title: The aegis
greek: nigrantem aegida concuteret dextra (8.354); aegidaque horriferam, turbatae Palladis arma (8.435)
short: The aegis is the goatskin storm-shield of Jupiter and Minerva, bearing the Gorgon's head; in this book Jove shakes it to raise storms and the Cyclopes polish Pallas' aegis.
body: The Greek aigis was originally a goatskin (aix, 'goat'), later imagined as a shield or breastplate fringed with snakes. Shaken by Zeus it raises storms and terror; in Iliad 5.738-742 Athena puts on the aegis with Fear, Strife and the Gorgon's head. Virgil uses both aspects in Book VIII: the Arcadians believe they have seen Jupiter on the Capitol shaking the 'darkening aegis' to gather storm-clouds (8.354), and in Vulcan's forge the Cyclopes burnish 'the awful aegis, the armour of wrathful Pallas', with golden serpent-scales and the severed Gorgon head with rolling eyes (8.435-438). It belongs to the arsenal of cosmic power that Vulcan sets aside to make Aeneas' arms.

sources.cite: C. T. Lewis and C. Short, A Latin Dictionary (Oxford, 1879), s.v. aegis

title: Mezentius' torture of the living bound to the dead
greek: mortua quin etiam iungebat corpora vivis / componens manibusque manus atque oribus ora
short: Evander describes Mezentius' cruelest torture: binding living men face to face and hand to hand with corpses so they died slowly in the rot.
body: This is the most horrifying detail in Mezentius' portrait and explains why his Etruscan subjects expelled him and now seek revenge. The practice had been ascribed by Aristotle to Etruscan pirates, as part of a famous comparison of the soul bound to the body; Virgil attaches it specifically to the tyrant Mezentius. G. Rosati discusses this 'long death' and how the torture works as a slow contagion of death. Evander's account justifies the Etruscan alliance with Aeneas, since Turnus has sheltered a tyrant; yet Book X will give Mezentius a moving death, so Virgil complicates even this villain.

sources.cite: Virgil, Aeneid 8.485, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)
G. Rosati, 'Euander's curse, and the "long death" of Mezentius (Aen. 8.483-488, 10.845-850)', Harvard Studies in Classical Philology (2017)
Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 1.2 (Mezentius king of Caere)

title: The Etruscan oracle: 'choose foreign leaders'
greek: nulli fas Italo tantam subiungere gentem: / externos optate duces
short: An Etruscan seer (haruspex) has told the Etruscans that no Italian may lead them against Mezentius; Evander, too old, passes the command to Aeneas.
body: This oracle mirrors Faunus' oracle to Latinus (7.96-101): in both cases Italy is told that a foreigner must come. The Etruscans were famous for divination, especially reading the entrails of sacrifices (the haruspices). Evander calls them 'chosen men of Maeonia', i.e. Lydia, because the Etruscans were believed to have come from Lydia in Asia Minor under Tyrrhenus (Herodotus 1.94); the 'Lydian race' settled 'on the Etruscan ridges' (8.479). Tarchon, their leader, has offered the crown to Evander, who declines because of age and because his son is half Sabine. Aeneas therefore acquires a great army by fate's design, not by conquest.

sources.cite: Virgil, Aeneid 8.499, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)
Herodotus 1.94 (the Lydian migration to Italy under Tyrrhenus)
C. T. Lewis and C. Short, A Latin Dictionary (Oxford, 1879), s.v. haruspex

title: Pallas like the Morning Star
greek: qualis ubi Oceani perfusus Lucifer unda, / quem Venus ante alios astrorum diligit ignis, / extulit os sacrum caelo tenebrasque resolvit
short: Young Pallas riding out at the head of the column is compared to the Morning Star, Venus' favourite, rising fresh from Ocean and dispelling darkness.
body: Lucifer ('light-bringer') is the planet Venus as morning star, beloved by Venus as goddess; the simile thus also hints at Aeneas' divine mother watching over the young man in his care. Homer compares Akhilleus' gleaming spear-point to the evening star (Iliad 22.317-318), just before Hector's death; Virgil's simile is equally beautiful and equally ominous. Evander's agonised farewell (8.560-583), praying to die before bad news can reach him, has already told readers what to fear. Pallas will be killed by Turnus in Book X, and his sword-belt will decide Turnus' fate at the end of Book XII.

title: The Shield of Aeneas
greek: et clipei non enarrabile textum. / illic res Italas Romanorumque triumphos / ... fecerat ignipotens
short: Vulcan's shield shows the future history of Rome from Romulus to Augustus' victory at Actium: a deliberate Roman answer to Homer's Shield of Akhilleus.
body: Homer's Shield of Akhilleus (Iliad 18.478-608) shows a timeless world: the cosmos, a city at peace and at war, farming and dancing. Virgil's shield shows Roman history in sequence, ordered by Conington as: the she-wolf; the Sabine women and the treaty; the punishment of Mettus; Porsenna repelled by Cocles and Cloelia; Manlius and the Gauls; Rome's religious rites; Catiline punished and Cato judging in the underworld; and, at the centre, Actium and Augustus' triumph. Conington defends Vulcan's foreknowledge ('not witless of prophecy'). The description is an ecphrasis (a verbal account of a work of art), and it is famously impossible to picture as a real shield, which the narrator half admits with non enarrabile ('beyond telling'). Aeneas understands none of it, yet carries it.

title: The she-wolf and the twins
greek: fecerat et viridi fetam Mavortis in antro / procubuisse lupam, geminos huic ubera circum / ludere pendentis pueros
short: The first scene on the shield shows the she-wolf in Mars' cave suckling Romulus and Remus and licking their bodies into shape.
body: Livy tells how the twins, sons of Mars and Rhea Silvia, were exposed on the Tiber and nursed by a she-wolf at the foot of the Palatine (1.4.6-7). The 'cave of Mars' is the Lupercal (8.343). Virgil's tender detail, the wolf bending back her neck to lick them in turn and 'shape their bodies with her tongue' (corpora fingere lingua), draws on the ancient belief that animals literally shaped their young by licking. The image was already a Roman emblem in Virgil's time (it appeared on coins and in bronze). Starting with this scene makes the shield begin, like the city, with a founding miracle.

title: Porsenna, Cocles and Cloelia
greek: nec non Tarquinium eiectum Porsenna iubebat / accipere ... cum pontem auderet vellere Cocles / et fluvium vinclis innaret Cloelia ruptis
short: The shield shows Lars Porsenna besieging Rome to restore the expelled Tarquin, and two heroes of the young republic: Horatius Cocles and Cloelia.
body: After the expulsion of the last king, Tarquinius Superbus, the Etruscan king Porsenna of Clusium tried to restore him (c. 508 BC). Horatius Cocles ('one-eyed') held the Sublician bridge alone while it was cut down behind him, then swam the Tiber in armour (Livy 2.10). Cloelia, a girl given as a hostage, escaped and swam the river with other hostages (Livy 2.13). Porsenna 'like one who chafes and like one who threatens' in a single snapshot: Virgil shows emotion in a frozen picture. These tales of liberty (pro libertate) celebrate the republic, an interesting choice on a shield that culminates in Augustus. Turnus' leap into the Tiber in full armour (9.815-818) may recall Cocles.

title: Manlius, the geese and the Gauls
greek: in summo custos Tarpeiae Manlius arcis ... / atque hic auratis volitans argenteus anser / porticibus Gallos in limine adesse canebat
short: Manlius guards the Capitol while the sacred geese of Juno raise the alarm against the Gauls climbing by night in 390 BC.
body: After the disaster at the Allia (7.717) the Gauls took Rome, but the Capitol held out. When they climbed it at night, the sacred geese of Juno woke M. Manlius, who threw the first Gaul down (Livy 5.47); he was named Capitolinus. The 'thatch of Romulus' palace' is the Casa Romuli, a hut preserved on the Capitol (and Palatine) as a relic. Virgil's metalwork is precise: a silver goose, Gauls with golden hair and golden torques, striped cloaks and Alpine javelins (gaesa). The irony that Manlius was later executed, thrown from the Tarpeian rock for seeking kingship, is not mentioned, though Roman readers knew it.

title: Catiline punished, Cato giving laws
greek: et te, Catilina, minaci / pendentem scopulo Furiarumque ora trementem, / secretosque pios, his dantem iura Catonem
short: In a corner of the shield, the underworld: the conspirator Catiline hangs from a cliff, terrified of the Furies, while Cato gives laws to the righteous apart.
body: L. Sergius Catilina led the conspiracy of 63 BC exposed by Cicero; he stands for the criminal threat to the Republic. Cato is almost certainly M. Porcius Cato the Younger, the Stoic who killed himself at Utica in 46 BC rather than live under Caesar. Conington accepts this identification and compares Cato's role to Minos as judge of the dead. It is striking that Virgil places Caesar's bitterest enemy in a position of honour on Augustus' shield: Cato had become a symbol of old Roman virtue that even the new regime could claim. The 'beetling rock' may suggest the Tarpeian rock, from which traitors were thrown. The scene echoes Book VI's division of the guilty and the good.

title: The Battle of Actium
greek: in medio classis aeratas, Actia bella, / cernere erat, totumque instructo Marte videres / fervere Leucaten
short: At the centre of the shield is the sea-battle of Actium (2 September 31 BC), where Octavian's fleet under Agrippa defeated Antony and Cleopatra.
body: Actium is a promontory at the mouth of the Ambracian Gulf in north-western Greece; Leucate is a headland nearby. Virgil turns a naval engagement into a cosmic clash between West and East, Roman gods and 'monstrous' Egyptian ones. Octavian stands on the stern with the Senate and People, the Penates and the great gods; Agrippa, his admiral, wears the naval crown decorated with ships' beaks (rostrata corona), an honour Conington notes he alone received. Antony brings 'barbarian aid and motley arms' and the Egyptian wife. The ships are so huge they look like the Cyclades floating loose. Conington's notes show how Virgil, Propertius and Horace all shaped Actium into Augustus' founding myth.

title: The Julian star (sidus Iulium)
greek: stans celsa in puppi, geminas cui tempora flammas / laeta vomunt patriumque aperitur vertice sidus
short: Augustus stands on the stern with twin flames from his temples and his 'ancestral star' above his head: the comet taken as the soul of the deified Julius Caesar.
body: In July 44 BC, during games held by Octavian in honour of the murdered Julius Caesar, a comet blazed for seven days; it was taken as Caesar's soul received among the gods (Suetonius, Divus Julius 88; Pliny, Natural History 2.93-94). Octavian placed a star on the head of Caesar's statues and on coins. Conington links the flames on the helmet to that comet and cites Eclogue 9.47 (the Caesaris astrum). The flames round the head also recall the omen of fire round Ascanius' head (2.680-691) and Lavinia's hair (7.71-80): a sign of divinely sanctioned destiny passing down the Julian line.

title: Cleopatra, the 'Egyptian wife'
greek: sequiturque (nefas) Aegyptia coniunx ... / regina in mediis patrio vocat agmina sistro, / necdum etiam geminos a tergo respicit anguis
short: Cleopatra is never named: she is the 'Egyptian wife' following Antony, rattling her sistrum and not yet seeing the two snakes of her death behind her.
body: Roman propaganda presented Actium as a war against a foreign queen, not a civil war against Antony. Virgil's parenthesis nefas ('horror!') captures Roman outrage that a Roman married an Egyptian. The sistrum, the rattle used in the worship of Isis, marks her as a foreign, Eastern religious figure; Conington notes she was portrayed as Isis. The 'twin snakes' foretell her suicide by asp-bite (Plutarch, Antony 86). Her flight, 'wan with the shadow of death', and the mourning Nile who opens his robes to receive the defeated, end the scene with a strange note of pity. Compare Horace's Cleopatra ode (Odes 1.37), which also moves from contempt to admiration, and Dido, the earlier African queen who loved a Trojan.

title: Anubis against Neptune, and Actian Apollo
greek: omnigenumque deum monstra et latrator Anubis / contra Neptunum et Venerem contraque Minervam / tela tenent ... / Actius haec cernens arcum intendebat Apollo / desuper
short: The battle is a war of gods: barking dog-headed Anubis and Egypt's monsters fight Neptune, Venus and Minerva, until Apollo of Actium draws his bow and the East flees.
body: Anubis, the Egyptian jackal-headed god, is called latrator, 'the barker', a contemptuous Roman view of animal-shaped gods (compare the 'vana superstitio' of 8.187). Mars, Discord and Bellona, the forces of war, rage in the middle. Apollo had an ancient temple on the promontory of Actium, and Octavian credited him with the victory, building the great temple of Apollo on the Palatine beside his house (dedicated 28 BC). Conington notes that Propertius (4.6) made Apollo the central figure at Actium and that the god acts 'from above' (desuper), from heaven or from his temple on the headland. The scene recalls the Gigantomachy, the gods' war against the Giants, a model of order defeating chaos.

title: Augustus' triple triumph and the conquered peoples
greek: at Caesar, triplici invectus Romana triumpho / moenia ... / Euphrates ibat iam mollior undis, / extremique hominum Morini, Rhenusque bicornis, / indomitique Dahae, et pontem indignatus Araxes
short: Augustus celebrates three triumphs, dedicates shrines throughout Rome and, seated at Apollo's temple, reviews a procession of conquered peoples and rivers.
body: In August 29 BC Octavian held triumphs on three successive days for Dalmatia, Actium and Egypt (Suetonius, Augustus 22); Conington cites this. The 'three hundred stately shrines' exaggerates his real programme of temple-building and restoration; Augustus claimed to have restored eighty-two temples in one year (Res Gestae 20). He sits at the 'snowy threshold' of Palatine Apollo, of gleaming white marble. The procession is a world map: Nomads and Africans, Leleges and Carians of Asia Minor, the Gelonians of Scythia, the Euphrates, with 'smoother waves', the Morini of the Channel coast, the 'two-horned' Rhine (with two mouths, as Conington explains), the Dahae beyond the Caspian, and the Araxes in Armenia 'chafing under his bridge'. Rivers in chains were carried in triumphs as images.

title: 'Attollens umero famamque et fata nepotum'
greek: talia per clipeum Volcani, dona parentis, / miratur rerumque ignarus imagine gaudet / attollens umero famamque et fata nepotum
short: Aeneas admires the shield without understanding it and lifts onto his shoulder the fame and destiny of his descendants.
body: The book ends on an image as famous as any in the poem. Aeneas is ignorant of the events (rerum ignarus) yet rejoices in their picture: Roman history is meaningful to Virgil's readers, who know it, but Aeneas can only take it on trust. The gesture of lifting the shield onto his shoulder recalls Aeneas carrying his father Anchises out of burning Troy on his shoulders (2.707-708, 721-723): then he carried his past, now he carries his people's future. Readers differ on the tone: some find triumphant confidence, others a lonely burden borne without comprehension. The next book, which shows the Trojan camp under siege without him, tests what that burden costs.
